config.title: Pipes — Creation & Usage

intro.title: Pipes — Creation & Usage
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll build a custom Angular pipe that formats currency values and learn how to use both built-in and custom pipes in templates. You'll explore the core concept of pipes, which are functions that transform data for display purposes without modifying the original data. The lesson covers creating a pipe class using the @Pipe decorator, implementing the PipeTransform interface, and applying pipes in component templates using the pipe operator (|). You'll work with Angular's dependency injection system and learn how to make pipes reusable across your application. By the end, you'll understand how pipes provide a clean separation between data transformation logic and component business logic.
intro.usecase: Angular pipes are essential for data transformation in modern web applications, appearing everywhere from e-commerce product listings that format prices and dates to social media feeds that display relative timestamps like '2 hours ago'. They're commonly used in admin dashboards to format currency values, user tables to transform usernames to proper case, and financial applications to display numbers with appropriate decimal places and thousand separators. Custom pipes become particularly valuable in enterprise applications where you need consistent data formatting across components, such as transforming API response data into user-friendly display formats or creating reusable filters for search results.

objectives: Implement a custom pipe class with transform method logic
Apply built-in Angular pipes to format data in component templates
Configure pipe parameters to control data transformation behavior
Integrate custom pipes into Angular module declarations
Construct pipe chains to perform multiple sequential data transformations
Bind pipe outputs to template expressions for dynamic data display
Manipulate pipe arguments to create reusable formatting utilities

steps.hint: Use the @Pipe decorator above the class declaration and specify the pipe name in the decorator options.

steps.title: Add pipe parameters and options
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph that displays the price using the currency pipe with 'USD' parameter and another paragraph that shows today's date using the date pipe with 'shortDate' format
steps.hint: Use the pipe parameter syntax with a colon and quotes - for example: value | pipeName:'parameter'. The currency pipe accepts currency codes like 'USD' and the date pipe accepts format strings like 'shortDate'.
steps.expectedOutcome: Two new paragraphs are added - one showing the formatted price with currency symbol and another showing the formatted date
successCriteria: Template includes a paragraph with price displayed using currency pipe with 'USD' parameter and a paragraph with today's date using date pipe with 'shortDate' parameter
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start with pipe parameters. Make sure you're using both the currency pipe with 'USD' for the price and the date pipe with 'shortDate' for the today property.
steps.feedbackWrong: use the pipe parameter syntax with a colon and quotes. Add {{ price | currency:'USD' }} for the price and {{ today | date:'shortDate' }} for the date.

steps.expectedOutcome: A complete NgModule with CapitalizePipe registered in the declarations array, making the custom pipe available for use in components.
successCriteria: NgModule decorator is added with CapitalizePipe included in the declarations array
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start on the module registration. Make sure to include the CapitalizePipe in the declarations array of the NgModule.
steps.feedbackWrong: The NgModule needs to be created with the @NgModule decorator and include CapitalizePipe in the declarations array to make the pipe available.
